name: Zulu Iziqu Necklace
material: Carved wood or bone blocks, fibre
description: The iziqu is the necklace of a Zulu warrior, made of carved wooden beads strung on a cord and worn across the chest as a mark of valour. After a king recognised a man for bravery in battle, the warrior was permitted to carve and string the necklace himself, usually from the wood of the thorn tree, and each row was said to record a heroic deed; Maclean, who saw the court of Shaka in 1825, described the necklaces as orders of merit conferred by the king's own hand. The iziqu was the second-highest decoration of the Zulu army after the brass armband (ingxotha), and the carved beads could be combined with bone, horn, and skin in protective war charms. The most famous string, the long wooden necklace of King Dinizulu, was taken by Robert Baden-Powell in 1888 and inspired the wooden beads of the Scout Wood Badge. A giant bronze iziqu crowns the Isandlwana monument honouring the Zulu army of 1879. Today the iziqu is remembered as one of the few personal honours a common warrior could win.

name: Zulu Iwisa Knobkerrie
description: The iwisa, often called the knobkerrie, is a Zulu club made from a single piece of hardwood, with a heavy round knob at the top of a straight or slightly curved handle. It was a close-combat weapon of the Zulu army, carried beside the spear and thrown or swung in the close fights of the impi, and it remained a warrior's constant companion when herding and walking. In peacetime the iwisa became a staff of rank: chiefs, headmen, and later officials carried finely carved examples, and the club is still raised in the air at ceremonies, weddings, and political gatherings as a gesture of authority. Craftsmen shaped the knob and handle with an adze and burnished them smooth, and the best pieces are polished to a deep shine. The knobkerrie has spread beyond the Zulu, serving as the famous weapon and walking stick of southern African leadership.

name: Zulu Ukhamba Beer Pot
description: The ukhamba is the clay beer pot of the Zulu, a round, low-necked vessel fired from local clay and used to brew and serve utshwala, the sorghum beer at the centre of Zulu hospitality. Beer is not everyday drink but the medium of ceremony: it is brewed by women, offered to the ancestors at the start of every gathering, and shared at marriages, funerals, and the community work-parties that bind homesteads together. The pot's shape is practical, the round belly holding the fermenting beer and the narrow mouth keeping it clean, and the clay keeps the beer cool. Well-made ukhamba are prized, and a woman's skill at brewing and presenting beer is a matter of family pride. Decorated pots, incised with patterns or fitted with beadwork covers, are made for important occasions, and Zulu pottery has been collected and exhibited as art. The ukhamba remains in daily use in KwaZulu-Natal alongside the woven beer-strainers and calabashes that complete the brewing set.

name: Xhosa Beadwork
description: Xhosa beadwork of South Africa is made with imported glass beads sewn onto leather, cotton, or cloth supports to create necklaces, aprons, headdresses, and panels of dress worn at the great passages of life. At initiation, the beads speak: the colours and patterns worn by a young man in the circumcision school, and by the women who celebrate his return, carry coded messages of love, status, and clan that are meant to be read by the initiated. Married women wear beadwork that records their lineage and their husband's house, while older styles of white and blue bands gave way to the bright colour families of the modern era. Beadwork was a woman's art, taught by mothers and grandmothers, and its patterns changed with fashion while keeping their social grammar. Today Xhosa beadwork is worn at weddings, initiation feasts, and church festivals, and the beaded garments of the Red Xhosa communities of the Eastern Cape remain the most photographed tradition. Cooperatives and designers now sell Xhosa beadwork across South Africa and abroad.

name: Mbira Dzavadzimu
description: The mbira dzavadzimu is the lamellophone of the Shona people of Zimbabwe, a wooden soundboard fitted with rows of metal keys and placed over a gourd resonator that buzzes with shells, bottle caps, or other rattling matter. Its name means 'mbira of the ancestor spirits', and it is played at the bira ceremonies where the spirits of the departed are called to advise the living. The interlocking patterns of the mbira weave around the singing and clapping of the assembly, and the buzzing, layered sound is thought to attract the spirits so that they can speak through a medium. The instrument is learned by hand within Shona families, and certain mbira pieces are held by specific lineages as inherited property. After independence the mbira became a national emblem of Zimbabwe, and its sound now opens radio broadcasts and accompanies church hymns. The instrument's deep, hypnotic cycles have also carried it into world music through Zimbabwean players and teachers.

name: Soapstone Bird of Great Zimbabwe
description: The soapstone birds of Great Zimbabwe are carved birds about 40 centimetres tall, with human lips, folded wings, and feet that grip the columns on which they once stood within the ruined stone city. Eight are known, six large and two small, and they are believed to have been royal emblems of the Shona state that built the city between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries, possibly representations of the bateleur eagle, the fish eagle, or a spirit bird of kingship. The birds probably crowned the walls and monoliths of the royal enclosure, marking the authority of the ruler, and the city itself gave its name to modern Zimbabwe. In the 1890s the carvings were hacked from their columns and carried to South Africa, where one passed into the hands of Cecil Rhodes; five birds were returned in 1981 and the last in 2026, ending more than a century of exile. The bird was adopted as Zimbabwe's national symbol in 1924 and appears on the flag, the coat of arms, and the country's coins.
source: Archaeological finds at Great Zimbabwe; UNESCO World Heritage

name: Chipendani Mouth Bow
description: The chipendani is a mouth bow of the Shona of Zimbabwe, a curved wooden stave with a single fibre or wire string, held against the open mouth and plucked so that the mouth shapes the tone. Because the cavity of the mouth acts as a resonator, the player can vary pitch and timbre while the string keeps up a light, rhythmic pattern. It is above all an instrument of herders and young men, who play it alone in the fields to pass the hours, to court, and to accompany themselves while singing. The chipendani is small and portable, carried in the hand or tucked in the belt, and its soft sound suits the quiet company of cattle rather than the crowd. Related mouth bows appear across southern Africa under different names. Although the mbira overshadowed it in the modern Shona music revival, the chipendani is still heard in the countryside and is taught in some schools and cultural programmes.

name: Lozi Royal Barge
description: The Lozi royal barge, the nalikwanda, is the great wooden vessel that carries the Litunga, the king of the Lozi people of western Zambia, at the Kuomboka ceremony. When the annual floods rise on the Zambezi, the king leaves the lowland palace and is paddled in procession to higher ground, the barge covered with an immense shroud of black-and-white cloth and surrounded by dozens of escort boats. The crossing is the climax of Kuomboka, a pageant that renews the bond between the king and the waters that shape Lozi life, and the barge's heavy, deliberate movement through the flood is timed to the songs of its rowers. The nalikwanda is built of timber by Lozi boatbuilders, and a new barge is commissioned when the old one fails. Kuomboka, whose name means 'to get out of the water', draws thousands of spectators each year. The barge is the central object of the most famous river festival in southern Africa.

name: Gule Wamkulu Mask
description: The gule wamkulu masks of the Chewa of Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique are carved wooden face masks worn by the dancers of the Nyau society, whose great dance of the same name is performed at initiations, funerals, and the memorials of the dead. Nyau means 'the big dance' or 'the dance of the spirits', and the masked dancers embody the ancestors, the animals of the bush, and the forces of the forest, revealing their meanings only to initiates. Each mask has a name and a character, the gentle, the comic, the terrible, and the dancer becomes the spirit while he wears it, speaking in its voice. The Nyau society, open only to initiated men, holds the history and the law of the Chewa, and the masks are stored in hidden groves away from women and strangers. UNESCO inscribed the gule wamkulu on the intangible heritage list in 2005. The tradition is still danced with force in the villages of the Chewa heartland.
source: Chewa Nyau tradition; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage

name: Makonde Lipiko Mask
description: The lipiko is the carved wooden mask of the Makonde people of northern Mozambique, worn by male dancers in the mapiko, a masked dance that forms part of the likumbi initiation rite marking the passage from puberty to adulthood. The mapiko performance, which UNESCO inscribed on its List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding in 2023 under the name Ingoma ya Mapiko, takes place in an open enclosure, often beneath mango trees, with dancers, drummers and a choir of men and women facing each other. The dancer's whole body is covered by the costume, and the mask, carved from a single block of wood and sometimes from scrap metal such as old cooking pots, shows a stylized face with pronounced lips and painted details, and is kept hidden from the uninitiated. Within the rite the masked dancer is held to embody the spirit of a dead ancestor, and the dance both solemnly stages the world of the dead and entertains the living, since it may also be danced at funerals of group members and for general celebration. Young Makonde men learn the making and wearing of masks and the steps of the dance during the secret initiation camp, with the knowledge passed down from elder carvers to the initiates.
